drills.q: Explain the classloader parent-delegation model and the concrete problem it prevents.
drills.a: Classloaders form a hierarchy (bootstrap -> platform -> application); each delegates a load request to its parent first before attempting to load the class itself. This guarantees core JDK classes (e.g. java.lang.String) always resolve to the trusted bootstrap-loaded version regardless of what an application or library defines with the same fully-qualified name, preventing malicious or accidental shadowing of core classes.

drills.q: Walk through interpreter -> C1 -> C2 tiered compilation and explain why the JVM doesn't just always compile with C2.
drills.a: Interpreter runs bytecode immediately with zero compile latency but slow dispatch. C1 compiles quickly with light optimization once a method crosses a low invocation threshold, giving fast throughput gains while gathering profiling data (branch outcomes, concrete types at call sites). C2 recompiles genuinely hot methods with aggressive, slower-to-produce optimizations informed by that profiling data. Always using C2 would maximize eventual throughput but pay expensive, slow compilation cost even for methods invoked only a handful of times -- terrible warmup latency.

drills.q: What is escape analysis, what two specific optimizations does it enable, and why is it restricted to the C2 tier?
drills.a: Escape analysis proves whether an allocated object can ever be referenced outside its allocating method or thread. Non-escape past the method enables scalar replacement (fields become local variables/registers, eliminating the heap allocation and its GC cost entirely). Non-escape past the thread enables lock elision (synchronized blocks are removed since no other thread could ever contend). It's C2-only because proving non-escape requires expensive whole-method, often cross-call data-flow analysis -- exactly the class of slow analysis reserved for methods that have proven themselves hot enough to be worth C2's compile-time budget.

drills.q: Compare G1 and generational ZGC on pause time, throughput, and memory, and state when you'd choose each.
drills.a: G1 (region-based, collects highest-garbage regions first) targets a configurable pause goal (commonly tens of ms) but still has real stop-the-world phases and can fall back to full GC. Generational ZGC achieves consistent sub-millisecond pauses (~0.1-0.5ms) independent of heap size via concurrent marking/relocation/remapping (colored pointers, load barriers), at the cost of no compressed object pointers (~15-30% more memory) and typically 5-15% lower throughput than G1. Choose G1 as the default for most services; choose generational ZGC specifically for large-heap, latency-SLO-bound workloads where pause consistency matters more than memory/throughput.

drills.q: What is a G1 humongous object, why does it hurt specifically, and how can you tune around it without switching collectors?
drills.a: An object larger than 50% of a region size is allocated specially across contiguous regions rather than fitting into a normal region. Workloads with frequent large allocations (big arrays/collections) suffer extra GC pressure and fragmentation from this special handling, since finding contiguous free regions is a harder bin-packing problem. Tuning lever: raising -XX:G1HeapRegionSize increases the humongous threshold (defined relative to region size), potentially converting previously-humongous allocations into normal regional ones -- though not a universal fix if object sizes vary too widely.

drills.q: A microbenchmark shows a method getting faster over its first several thousand calls before stabilizing. Explain the cause and the correct way to measure it.
drills.a: JIT warmup -- early calls run interpreted or C1-compiled, and once the method crosses C2's invocation threshold and gets recompiled with aggressive optimization (possibly including escape analysis and speculative inlining), performance stabilizes at steady-state C2-optimized levels. Measure with JMH, which explicitly separates warmup iterations (discarded) from measurement iterations and guards against dead-code elimination/constant-folding via blackholes -- a hand-rolled System.nanoTime() loop conflates warmup cost with steady-state performance and doesn't guard against those pitfalls.

drills.q: A hot method's latency regresses sharply and permanently mid-run in production. What's your hypothesis and how do you confirm it?
drills.a: C2 likely deoptimized the method -- a speculative assumption broke (a previously-monomorphic call site became polymorphic, a class was redefined, an array-bounds-check-elimination assumption was violated), discarding the compiled code and falling back to the interpreter. Confirm via JFR (Java Flight Recorder) or -XX:+PrintCompilation/-XX:+TraceDeoptimization correlated with the regression timestamp. If the pattern causing deopt persists, the method may thrash between compilation and deopt ('deopt storm') -- the fix is usually addressing the polymorphism at the call site, not JVM flags.

drills.q: Your service on G1 shows acceptable average latency but a p99.9 tail with 200-400ms spikes correlated with GC logs. Walk through the diagnosis and options in order of invasiveness.
drills.a: First correlate spikes precisely against GC log timestamps to confirm whether they're young, mixed, or full GCs (full GC is the likeliest culprit for 200-400ms+ pauses), and check for humongous-object allocation or fragmentation contributing to full-GC fallback. Then: tune G1 first (realistic MaxGCPauseMillis, heap/region sizing, address humongous allocation patterns); if that can't close the gap and the SLO is genuinely violated, evaluate generational ZGC for its sub-ms pause guarantee, accepting the throughput/memory cost; in parallel, reduce allocation rate at the source (pooling, escape-analysis-friendly code shapes) since lower allocation pressure helps under either collector.

drills.q: Escape analysis 'should' eliminate an allocation given the source code shape, but profiling shows it's still heap-allocating. Diagnose.
drills.a: First confirm the method actually reached C2 compilation (-XX:+PrintCompilation) since escape analysis is C2-only and unavailable to the interpreter or C1. If it did compile with C2, look for an escape path not obvious from a quick read -- the object passed to a logging call, stored conditionally in a collection, or captured by a lambda/closure that itself escapes. Even one rarely-executed escaping code path defeats scalar replacement for the entire allocation site.

drills.q: Is ZGC's claim of pause time independent of heap size the same as saying GC work itself is free at large heap sizes? Explain.
drills.a: No. Pause time being independent of heap size is a genuine, correctly-cited design property (unlike traditional stop-the-world collectors where pause time scales with live-set size) -- but the concurrent marking/relocation work ZGC does still consumes CPU proportional to live data and allocation rate. That ongoing concurrent cost is exactly where ZGC's throughput deficit versus G1 (typically 5-15% lower) comes from, even though it never shows up as a long stop-the-world pause.
